title: Garden Centre Plant Finder
story: A garden centre kiosk suggests plants as a customer types: after each letter it shows up to three plant names starting with the letters so far, in alphabetical order. The catalogue merges several suppliers, so a name can be listed more than once, but the kiosk never shows a name twice in one set of suggestions.
task: Write suggestPlants(catalogue, typed). For each i from 1 to typed.length, take the first i letters of typed and find the distinct catalogue names that start with them. Return a list with one entry per letter typed: the alphabetically first three of those names, or fewer if fewer exist, or an empty list if none do.
A name that equals the typed letters exactly counts as starting with them.
constraints: 1 ≤ typed.length ≤ 30, and every name is 1 to 30 letters long
Only lowercase letters a to z.

examples.explanation: After "m": five names match; the first three alphabetically are magnolia, maple, marigold. After "ma": the same three (mint and moss drop out). After "map": only maple.
fern is listed twice but shown once. After "f": fern, fig, fuchsia. After "fe": fern. After "fex": nothing matches.

hints: Compare the suggestions for "m" and "ma" in the first example. Can a name not starting with "m" ever appear for "ma"? What does each extra letter do to the candidates?
Each letter can only narrow the candidates. In a sorted catalogue, where do all the names starting with "ma" sit relative to each other?
Names sharing a beginning share a path in a trie. Could each trie node remember the answer for its own prefix?

Sort the catalogue and drop duplicates. Insert the names into a trie in that order; at every node you pass, append the name if the node's list has fewer than 3 entries. Then walk typed letter by letter, reading each node's list. Once a letter has no child, every later answer is an empty list.
bruteForce: For each prefix of typed, scan the whole catalogue, keep the matches, remove duplicates, sort and take three. That is O(L · n log n) for L typed letters and n names, repeated from scratch per keystroke. A kiosk wants each keystroke to cost the same small amount whatever the catalogue size.

walkthrough: Every prefix of typed is a node in a trie of the catalogue. If each node already knows its three alphabetically first names, a keystroke is one step down plus a read.
To fill those lists, insert the names in alphabetical order. The first three names through a node are then its three smallest, so each node keeps the first three it sees.
Trace the first example. Sorted: lavender, magnolia, maple, marigold, mint, moss.
• lavender fills the l-branch. magnolia passes m and ma: both lists get magnolia.
• maple passes m, ma, map: m and ma hold [magnolia, maple]; map holds [maple].
• marigold passes m and ma: both lists are now full.
• mint and moss pass m, whose list is full, so they are skipped there.
• Typing "map": read m → [magnolia, maple, marigold], ma → the same, map → [maple].
Removing duplicates first means a name never fills two slots. And once a letter has no child, the walk is off the trie for good: later letters cannot bring matches back.

Without a trie, use the sorted list from hint 2: names with a prefix sit together, so binary search for the first name ≥ the prefix and check up to three from there. That is O(log n · S) per keystroke instead of O(1), with no extra structure.
solution.timeWhy: Sorting n names of up to S letters dominates the build; each keystroke afterwards is one child lookup and a read.
solution.spaceWhy: One trie node per letter inserted, each holding at most three names.
solution.takeaway: When every prefix needs its own answer, store the answer in the trie node for that prefix. Inserting items in sorted order lets each node keep "the first few" without any extra sorting.
